articles.title: China’s Unity Through Erasure Should Worry Central Asia
articles.full_text:
The SCO may serve legitimate Central Asian interests, but it should not become the vehicle through which Beijing’s definitions of security, political loyalty, and ethnic identity become normalized across the Turkic world.
China’s growing efforts to increase control over the Turkic states of Central Asia was the dominant, if little discussed, outcome of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan on September 1. 
Beijing wants its relationship with the Central Asian states to be one of vassals thankful for China’s “protection” and economic integration. The recent summit produced the 25th anniversary Bishkek Declaration and 27 other documents, which claimed they would strengthen mechanisms for security, countering terrorism and organized crime, and promised new transport lines and logistics. On its face, the Central Asian states are promised infrastructure, technology and diplomatic engagement. But beneath those promises is guaranteed deeper dependence on Chinese capital, standards, and security concepts.
China successfully got Muslim-majority states (including Iran, Pakistan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, and Uzbekistan) to sign onto documents clearly aimed at China’s own Turkic Muslim populations. The SCO endorsement of combatting “terrorism, separatism, and extremism” was China-sponsored and indisputably about Uyghurs. Under this pretext, the institutional capacity that enables surveillance, intelligence exchange, and political labeling of Uyghurs is being expanded.
Sadly, China’s economic leverage and coercion means the public support that these Muslim-majority states provide to Muslim communities globally is absent when it comes to China. 
The Central Asian states should ponder carefully when Beijing uses the security vocabulary noted in the Bishkek Declaration. China’s decade-long ethnic cleansing campaign in Xinjiang, also referred to as East Turkestan, demonstrates what happens when cultural difference is reclassified as a security problem. Religious behavior can be labelled extremism. Cultural autonomy can be called separatism. Overseas relationships of Uyghurs with Turkic states have tended to attract suspicion. Language, memory, and identity become objects of political management.
ASPI’s Xinjiang Data Project has documented mass detention, surveillance, forced labor and political re-education. ASPI’s Cultural Erasure research estimated that around 16,000 of Xinjiang’s 24,000 mosques had been damaged or destroyed, alongside extensive damage to Islamic shrines and other sacred sites central to regional Turkic history. Arguments that Beijing is only concerned about its “ internal affairs” are blind to China’s foreign policy.
Beijing’s formula of combating the “three evils” – terrorism, separatism, and extremism – was incorporated into the SCO establishment document signed in June 2001, and that vocabulary has been institutionalized across Eurasia.
That should matter in the Muslim-majority Turkic states of Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, and Turkiye. 
During Xi’s visit to Kyrgyzstan, Bishkek explicitly reaffirmed support for China on Xinjiang-related issues while agreeing to deepen law-enforcement, counterterrorism, and information-security cooperation. China and Uzbekistan have made similar commitments.
Uyghur, Kazakh, Kyrgyz, Uzbek, and other Turkic identities do not end at borders. Families, languages, religious traditions, and diaspora communities extend across the region. When governments repeat Beijing’s anti-separatist language without qualification, they risk allowing legitimate concern for fellow Turkic communities to be recast as interference or subversion.
China’s July 2026 Law on the Promotion of Ethnic Unity and Progress contains a provision on extraterritoriality (Article 63) that authorizes Chinese authorities to pursue organizations and individuals outside of China’s borders. 
China’s recent technological advancements increase the risks that might have been assessed in 2001 by the SCO founding nations (Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, and Uzbekistan) as unlikely to cross borders. Some Chinese tech companies expanding across Central Asia have developed important capabilities within the same security ecosystem used to monitor and suppress Uyghurs and other Turkic peoples in the region.
iFLYTEK worked with China’s Ministry of Public Security on voiceprint systems and supplied voice-recognition technology used by Xinjiang police. It has since established a Central Asian presence in Tashkent offering multilingual AI services.
Technical documentation from Dahua policing systems described functions including “real-time Uyghur warnings” and identification of Uyghur attributes. Dahua disputes allegations that it intentionally designed systems for ethnic targeting. But its technology demonstrates how ostensibly neutral surveillance platforms can be adapted for ethnicity-based policing. Dahua systems are already present in Central Asian security environments.
Genomics raises an equally serious question of sovereignty. BGI has established sequencing capabilities in Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan and has discussed combining AI with large-scale genomic data in Central Asia. Those laboratory platforms are likely to be connected and operate on Beijing’s cyber cloud, in collaboration with companies such as Huawei. But genomic information is permanent, sensitive, and strategically valuable. The Central Asian states should know where samples are processed, where data is stored, who can access it, and whether it can leave national jurisdiction.
The same scrutiny should apply to natural resources.
Chinese entities are expanding into geological exploration, mining, and processing across Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan, Tajikistan, and Kyrgyzstan. Joint surveys can give Chinese partners detailed knowledge of strategic mineral deposits long before extraction begins. The China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway will bring genuine commercial benefits, but it will also strengthen Beijing’s overland supply chains and reduce China’s dependence on vulnerable maritime routes.
The answer for the Central Asian SCO members is not decoupling from China as there is a genuine need for infrastructure, capital, technology, and markets to boost living standards. But blindly accepting and complying with Beijing’s demands is also not what a sovereign state should aim for. The Russian invasion of Ukraine has heightened anxiety across the former Soviet republics and encouraged Central Asian states to diversify their external relationships, including by moving closer to Beijing. But that strategic realignment should not proceed without regard to China’s human rights in general and to Xinjiang specifically. The experience of Uyghurs and other Turkic peoples under Chinese rule offers a stark warning about the political costs that can accompany deeper dependence on Beijing.
Turkic governments should distinguish violent terrorism from peaceful political advocacy, religious practice, and diaspora activity. They should scrutinize Chinese surveillance and AI systems, protect biometric and genomic data, retain sovereign control over strategic geological information, and strengthen protections against transnational repression.
The SCO may serve legitimate Central Asian interests, but it should not become the vehicle through which Beijing’s definitions of security, political loyalty, and ethnic identity become normalized across the Turkic world.

articles.title: Is China Really a Cyber Threat to Taiwan?
articles.full_text:
Most people assume that China’s cyber capabilities define the totality of its threat to Taiwan, but this simply does not capture the full picture.
In July, Taiwan witnessed a first-of-its-kind intrusion – a sophisticated AI cyberattack against its government and private sector networks. The hack was suspected to have been carried out by Chinese actors. While impactful, this is not surprising and it overinflates perceptions of China’s true cyber threat to Taiwan. 
Most people assume that China’s cyber capabilities define the totality of its threat to Taiwan, but this simply does not capture the full picture. Intent and opportunity to use cyber are equally critical. A threat is properly defined as the product of an adversary’s intent, opportunity, and capability. While China’s cyber capabilities currently pose a significant threat to Taiwan’s digital sovereignty, environmental factors limit its intent and opportunity to use cyber in an existential way toward Taiwan. The threat is currently modest but can change rapidly as conditions shift.
Taiwan represents a fundamental challenge for China’s leadership, not only due to its dominance over the semiconductor market, but also due to its mere existence as a democracy made up of ethnic Chinese. The Chinese Communist Party (CCP) risks losing legitimacy with its populace – and its power – if Taiwan is not incorporated back into the mainland. Thus, China has indicated it aims to integrate Taiwan back into China by 2049. 
The most likely scenario under which China would use cyber in a catastrophic way toward Taiwan would be if it were coupled with an invasion or blockade of Taiwan. Cyber is one of the many tools in the toolbox for states, and like other military actions, its goal is to induce a political outcome. A digital blockade, for instance, through a series of massive multi-sector cyberattacks, by itself would likely not be China’s first coercive option to induce reunification. A naval blockade would likely have a much more sizable and lengthy impact than a digital blockade. Unlike physical ships that cannot be moved unless sunken or moved, a cyberspace effect’s lifespan is much shorter. 
Cyber impact often takes time to generate, requiring complex access and capabilities to be developed, all the while remaining undetected. Once cyber is leveraged against a target, it can be difficult to meaningfully re-engage the target to produce sufficient follow-on impact. After the first cyber shot is fired, network and systems administrators work rapidly to identify vulnerabilities, like the access pathways and malware used. They then reconstitute their network, bringing it back online and patching any remaining known vulnerabilities. While malware can be retooled and new access vectors generated, this too can take time and slow down the offensive inertia. This is why cyber is often more impactful when coupled with other forms of statecraft, not just as a standalone instrument.
China does not currently intend to reunify with Taiwan through force. The costs associated with a kinetic invasion are estimated to be in the trillions of dollars, with impact on the global economy upwards of 10 percent of world-wide GDP. China would bear a significant portion of the costs, including long-term repercussions on its other national goals. Consequently, China has generated an alternate strategy beyond kinetic means to reunify.
That isn’t to say that China won’t take cyber actions against Taiwan. But the threat as it currently exists is not an existential one. 
Central to China’s cyber program is its emphasis on securing information superiority. Whoever controls the information environment controls the levers of power and a population’s political preferences. China utilizes cyber tools daily to gradually chip away at the will of the Taiwanese, aiming to normalize its malicious actions. According to the Taiwanese government, Chinese cyber actors attempt 2.6 million intrusions of its critical infrastructure networks every day. Over a prolonged period, China believes it can both routinely influence the Taiwanese populace to rejoin the mainland while preparing for kinetic reunification as a last-resort effort.
Polling indicates that only 5 percent of Taiwanese want to unify with the mainland. Peaceful reunification currently seems highly unplausible. While cracks are apparent in the Taiwanese political apparatus, they are not substantial enough to tip the scales in China’s favor in any meaningful way. However, Chinese leadership does not appear publicly frustrated by its slow progress in Taiwan, likely due to its long-term strategic outlook. Thus, it will likely continue its peaceful approach, unless something drastic occurs, such as a change to the United States’ “One China” policy or if Taiwan declares its independence publicly.
Taiwan’s critical infrastructure is clearly vulnerable to attack. Both technical and nontechnical security gaps in Taiwan provide China ample access vectors and freedom to traverse through Taiwan’s cyberspace, sometimes undetected. China values secrecy in its cyber operations against Taiwan and uses techniques such as “living-off-the-land” to clandestinely move from network to network and deep inside critical systems. 
Taiwan is one of the world’s most digitally connected countries which increases its cyberspace risk despite its economic upsides. Due to Taiwan’s heavy reliance on imported energy, at over 96 percent, ports like Taichung and Kaohsiung become strategic weaknesses. Impacting even one of these ports could generate downstream effects for Taiwan’s economy and societal functioning. Additional chokepoints include Taiwan’s reliance on only 15 subsea cables for its digital connectivity, as well as its heavily centralized water and electricity networks. All of these are potential targets in a major cyberattack scenario, given China’s years of posturing for conflict.
While Taiwan is clearly vulnerable from a cyberspace perspective, other factors significantly reduce China’s opportunity to threaten Taiwan existentially in cyberspace. As articulated earlier, an invasion or blockade are the only other two realistic options that would likely necessitate China using major cyber action against Taiwan. However, even a blockade may have its political limits toward accomplishing unification. While a blockade or digital blockade would present dire circumstances for Taiwan, historically, blockades have not led to countries capitulating their sovereignty. Current polling indicates that between 50 to 85 percent of Taiwanese would politically resist coercion by China’s military in an attempt for unification. Taiwan’s resolve and international backing would likely outweigh China’s prolonged blockade.
Beyond blockades, true political unification in Taiwan will require boots-on-the-ground to unite the two countries. However, there is speculation that China is not currently ready to conduct a full-scale invasion or a blockade of Taiwan. For a military invasion, the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) must be able to conduct a complex inter-service amphibious landing from over 100 nautical miles away and pacify an unwilling population while securing logistics lines and staving off any counter-intervention forces. The PLA’s lack of reliable leadership, unproven joint operations, and nonexistent recent combat experience indicates it is likely not ready to conduct a full joint island attack campaign anytime soon. 
Thus, the opportunity for China to threaten Taiwan through a major cyber incident as a part of a larger coercive unification strategy in the current moment is negligible. 
China has likely caught up to the United States in cyberspace and is now a world-class cyber superpower, able to operate at speed and scale. China’s offensive cyber program will only become harder to counter in the future with the development of advanced AI models. From a capabilities perspective, China currently has the technology, pre-positioned malware, people, and technical expertise to carry out a major cyberattack against Taiwan. 
There are over 100 malicious cyber actors that operate out of China. According to former FBI Director Christopher Wray, China possesses 50 times more hackers than the FBI’s cyber professionals. China clearly invests heavily in its cyber force, likely due to its importance in its overall Taiwan and information dominance strategy. 
Beyond sheer force size, rapid advancements in AI capabilities are occurring daily and will likely give adversaries like China a first-mover advantage. China is already on the front lines of advanced AI model development, and any application to offensive cyber will completely redefine the cyber threat landscape for Taiwan. Many already predict that AI will provide cyber attackers the upper hand over cyber defenders in the short term.
There was a suspected Chinese-origin AI cyberattack of Taiwan in July. If true, this may indicate that China is making the leap from offensive cyber research and design to integration and deployment. While China has a long record of pre-positioning malware globally, AI will likely assist its cyber operators with breaking into traditionally hard-to-hack networks like air gapped industrial control systems and supervisory control and data acquisition (ICS/SCADA), defense, and government networks. Taiwan’s cyber defenses are likely not as advanced as compared to China’s capabilities, given China’s global superiority in the offensive cyberspace. 
Thus, China meets all the necessary capabilities requirements to cause Taiwan’s networks serious harm.
While China’s capabilities are formidable and amplify its potential to cause Taiwan harm, they are muted by significant environmental factors. The magnitude of threats often change, and the threat model used provides only a snapshot in time for China’s current cyber threat. It is not an eternal label. 
China will likely only be a modest threat overall temporarily. When future conditions are ripe, China will pose a much graver threat to Taiwan’s existence as a free and digitally sovereign society than it currently does. 
While one cannot predict what will happen next, Taiwan can take steps now to preserve its digital sovereignty and future as a free nation. It can  develop a whole-of-society AI Cyber Shield to offset offensive AI cyber capabilities, and train more government cyber operators and establish national cyber privateers. That includes conducting red team cyberattacks on critical infrastructure chokepoints.
Taiwan can increase societal resilience to mass cyber shock, continue civil-military joint readiness exercises, and prepare hack-back offensive plans and capabilities.
Finally, Taiwan can improve foreign partner engagement to glean best cybersecurity practices.
Taiwan may currently be in a suitable state to survive China’s low-level cyber influence campaign, but the future is much less assured. China has and continues to prepare itself for conflict to unify with Taiwan. If Taiwan does not take the appropriate steps to secure its cyberspace, a day will come when the threat becomes reality. Perhaps then China will be the ten-foot-tall cyber giant everyone presumes it to be.
In July, Taiwan witnessed a first-of-its-kind intrusion – a sophisticated AI cyberattack against its government and private sector networks. The hack was suspected to have been carried out by Chinese actors. While impactful, this is not surprising and it overinflates perceptions of China’s true cyber threat to Taiwan. 
Most people assume that China’s cyber capabilities define the totality of its threat to Taiwan, but this simply does not capture the full picture. Intent and opportunity to use cyber are equally critical. A threat is properly defined as the product of an adversary’s intent, opportunity, and capability. While China’s cyber capabilities currently pose a significant threat to Taiwan’s digital sovereignty, environmental factors limit its intent and opportunity to use cyber in an existential way toward Taiwan. The threat is currently modest but can change rapidly as conditions shift.
Taiwan represents a fundamental challenge for China’s leadership, not only due to its dominance over the semiconductor market, but also due to its mere existence as a democracy made up of ethnic Chinese. The Chinese Communist Party (CCP) risks losing legitimacy with its populace – and its power – if Taiwan is not incorporated back into the mainland. Thus, China has indicated it aims to integrate Taiwan back into China by 2049. 
The most likely scenario under which China would use cyber in a catastrophic way toward Taiwan would be if it were coupled with an invasion or blockade of Taiwan. Cyber is one of the many tools in the toolbox for states, and like other military actions, its goal is to induce a political outcome. A digital blockade, for instance, through a series of massive multi-sector cyberattacks, by itself would likely not be China’s first coercive option to induce reunification. A naval blockade would likely have a much more sizable and lengthy impact than a digital blockade. Unlike physical ships that cannot be moved unless sunken or moved, a cyberspace effect’s lifespan is much shorter.
articles.summary: Most people assume that China’s cyber capabilities define the totality of its threat to Taiwan, but this simply does not capture the full picture.

articles.title: Indonesia Reopens Airports After Suspension Due to Volcanic Eruption
articles.full_text:
The eruption of Anak Krakatau, which is located on a small island in the Sunda Strait, forced the closure of eight airports, including two serving the capital Jakarta.
Lava spews from Anak Krakatau, a volcano in the Sunda Strait between the Indonesian islands of Java and Sumatra, during an eruption on Oct. 20, 2018.
Indonesia reopened five airports early this morning, after a volcanic eruption over the weekend forced them to suspend operations for two days.
Anak Krakatau, which is located on a small island in the Sunda Strait between the islands of Java and Sumatra, began erupting late on Friday and remained active for around 25 hours.
The eruption threw up black plumes of volcanic ash that were carried by the wind over the skies of the capital, Jakarta, which lies around 150 kilometers to the east, and across Lampung province in the southern part of Sumatra.
This forced the closure of eight airports, including two servicing Jakarta. As the BBC reported, “snaking queues had formed at the departure halls in Jakarta’s Soekarno-Hatta International Airport on Monday as stranded passengers sought refunds and tried to get updates on when they would be able to fly.” Indonesian officials said yesterday that 2,961 flights were disrupted, leaving around 341,000 people stranded.
In a statement today, Transport Minister Dudy Purwagandhi said that Jakarta’s Soekarno-Hatta International Airport, the capital’s primary airport, resumed operations this morning after wind blew the ash away from the ⁠vicinity, Reuters reported. Four other airports, including a smaller one in Jakarta and another in the neighboring city of ​Bandung, also reopened today. Two airports remain closed, while one resumed operations yesterday.
Dudy ​told reporters that authorities would now need to confirm the airworthiness of the 178 aircraft that were at Soekarno-Hatta during ‌the closure. “Perhaps it’ll ⁠take some little extra time to prepare the planes,” he said.

It has been sporadically active for much of the last decade, and an eruption in 2018 caused a devastating tsunami that killed hundreds of people and displaced tens of thousands.

articles.title: Letters Targeting Kashmiri Pandits Surface on Social Media
articles.full_text:
The letters have revived memories of “hit lists” that Islamist militant groups issued in 1989-90.
An abandoned house belonging to Kashmiri Pandits in Anantnag district, Jammu and Kashmir, India.
Letters threatening Kashmiri Pandits that surfaced on social media in August have set off a wave of panic among members of the community living in Jammu and Kashmir (J&K). They have revived memories of the “hit lists” and assassinations that forced around 350,000 Pandits to flee the Kashmir valley over 36 years ago.
Three letters, all issued in the name of the United Liberation Council (ULC), said to be a front organization of the Pakistan-based Lashkar-e-Taiba, have surfaced on social media so far. The most recent letter, dated August 27, was explicitly linked to the Indian government reopening investigations into the massacre of Pandits by Islamist militants at the height of the anti-India militancy in the 1990s.
“If the SIA [State Investigation Agency of J&K] or any other agency is so eager to reopen closed cases involving migrant Pandits, they should also investigate cases like Bijebehara, Gawkadal, Sopore, Handwara, etc., where the so-called Indian mercenary security forces deliberately opened fire on innocent Kashmiris,” the letter said. “We will slaughter all those involved in these crimes no matter how much security they have.”
The first letter, dated August 7, named six Pandits working in the J&K government’s revenue department and included their cell phone numbers. It called on them to “change their ways.” The second letter, dated August 23, named six more Pandits and provided their residential addresses, including house numbers and street names. It described them as “white collar terrorists” and “traitors,” working for their “masters” in Delhi.
The letter’s contents were ominous. “Wherever you are and wherever you go, we are watching your every move,” it said. While the August 7 letter named Pandits working in the valley, the August 23 post listed Pandits in Jammu.
Kashmiri Pandits are Hindus and indigenous to the Muslim-dominated Kashmir valley. At the start of the militancy in 1989-1990, several Pandits, including Tika Lal Taploo, Neelkanth Ganjoo, Sarwanand Koul Premi and Virender Koul were assassinated. Sarla Bhat, a nurse, was abducted, raped and killed. Although militants claimed they were killed for their links to the Indian state – Taploo was a politician and Ganjoo was a high court judge—amid the rising tide of Islamism in Kashmir, it caused immense fear among the Pandits.
In an article I wrote for The Diplomat in 2020, I recounted what Ashok Dhar, a Pandit previously living in Baramulla in the valley, told me about what happened in 1989-90. “It was evident that Kashmiri Muslims wanted us to leave the Valley,” he recalled. Militant groups like the Jammu and Kashmir Liberation Front and the Hizbul Mujahideen brought out “hit lists” with names of Pandits to be eliminated. People shouted anti-Pandit slogans in mosques and at rallies. “They wanted sharia rule in Kashmir,” Dhar said, adding that Pandits were given a choice to convert to Islam or leave the valley.
Around 70,000 Pandit families comprising over 350,000 women, men, and children fled the valley in 1990. Dhar and his family were among them.
Most of the Pandits who left the Kashmir valley were subsequently housed in migrant camps in Jammu and Delhi. Many settled in other Indian cities. Most of them have never returned home. A few hundred families remained in the valley.
In its letters, the JLC has distinguished between those who remained in the valley and those who left. It is the latter that it is targeting now, the letters say.
While for most part, Pandits in the valley were left unharmed over the decades, Islamist militants have targeted the community periodically. The Lashkar-e-Taiba and the Hizbul Mujahideen massacred 23 Pandits, including four children, at Wandhama in 1997 and another 24 Pandits, including two children, at Nadimarg in 2003.
Memories of the terror they experienced remain deeply etched in the memory of Pandits.
Soon after the second letter emerged, Dhar, who now lives in Bengaluru, spoke to The Diplomat. The JLC’s lists providing names and other identifying details of Pandits “are no different from the hit lists of 1990,” he said.
Since 2008, when former Prime Minister Manmohan Singh announced a rehabilitation package, New Delhi has promised government jobs, cash doles, accommodation and security to Pandits returning to the valley. Yet this has not been enough to convince them to return in large numbers.
Continuing attacks on Pandits in the valley – in October 2021, for example, a pharmacist who stayed back in Srinagar, J&K’s capital, in 1990, was shot dead – have kept the community on tenterhooks. The government may have provided returning Pandits with tight security but since they live in clusters, they fear they are sitting ducks for Islamist militants.
In recent months, New Delhi has reopened investigations into several high-profile murders and massacres by militant groups in Kashmir. Among the cases that have been reopened are the rape and murder of Sarla Bhat, and the massacre at Wandhama.
These investigations could serve to meet the demands of Kashmiri Pandit organizations that have been demanding justice. But also, they will reopen old wounds.
Meanwhile, this is sure to prompt Kashmiri Muslims to demand justice in incidents of mass killings by the Indian security forces. The ULC referred to this in its third letter. “It appears to be positioning itself as a guardian of Kashmiri Muslim interests. But Kashmiris, “even the Muslims, are unlikely to be impressed as they have suffered for decades, even as the militant groups operated from the safety of camps in Pakistan,” Dhar said.
When two non-Kashmiri Indian laborers working at a brick kiln in Kulgam district in the valley were shot dead on July 31, analysts pointed out that militants were hitting “soft targets” as they were not strong enough to take on India’s security forces. The targeting of Pandit civilians is yet another example of militants seeking to assert their presence by intimidating unarmed people.
Should the letters prompt Pandits to leave again, it will deal a blow to New Delhi’s efforts to normalize the situation in J&K.

articles.title: Cambodia Confirms Resumption of Joint Military Exercises With US Next Year
articles.full_text:
The move reflects the sea change that has taken place in U.S.-Cambodia relations under the second Trump administration.
U.S. Navy Adm. Steve Koehler, commander of the U.S. Pacific Fleet (center left), U.S. Charge d’Affaires to Cambodia Aleks Zittle (right), and Royal Cambodian Navy Rear Adm. Mey Dina, commander of the Ream Naval Base (center right), pose for a photo with their staff during Koehler’s visit to the base in Sihanoukville, Cambodia, Aug. 7, 2026.
Cambodia’s army has confirmed that it will resume joint military exercises with the United States early next year after a decade-long suspension, the latest sign of the improving ties between the two nations.
The Royal Cambodian Army announced on Facebook on Friday that officials from the two nations had concluded an Initial Planning Conference for Exercise Angkor Sentinel 2027, which it said would be held in February of next year.
The exercise has the aim of “strengthening interoperability and disaster-response capabilities, reflecting renewed momentum in Cambodia–U.S. military cooperation and a shared commitment to strengthening defense cooperation.”
The announcement follows several high-level meetings between U.S. and Cambodian officials. These include a meeting last month between Prime Minister Hun Manet and Elbridge A. Colby, undersecretary for policy at the U.S. Department of War, during which the two discussed expanded defense cooperation.
Hun Manet said at the time that he was satisfied with the “positive momentum in Cambodia-U.S. relations” and the ongoing talks about the resumption of Angkor Sentinel, the Associated Press reported. “The joint exercises and training not only build military capability but also serve as a vital bridge to foster close friendship between the armed forces of both countries,” he added.
This was not long after Adm. Steve Koehler, commander of the U.S. Pacific Fleet, traveled to Phnom Penh for meetings with officials including Gen. Vong Pisen, the commander-in-chief of the Royal Cambodian Armed Forces, and Vice Adm. Tea Sokha, the commander of the Royal Cambodian Navy.
The visit “reaffirmed the United States’ long-term commitment to strengthening bilateral relationships and partnerships that advance a shared vision for a free and open Indo-Pacific,” the U.S. Pacific Fleet said in a statement at the time.
Angkor Sentinel was held for the first time in 2010 but was unilaterally canceled by the Cambodian government in early 2017, shortly after Cambodian troops took part for the first time in Golden Dragon, a joint military exercise with the Chinese military. The move reflected the mutually reinforcing deterioration of Phnom Penh’s relations with Washington and its growing proximity to China.
The resumption of the exercise has been anticipated by both sides for some time. It was first publicly discussed in early 2025, just prior to President Trump’s return to the White House, and has been referenced in most high-level diplomatic meetings since then. It reflects the sea change that has taken place in U.S.-Cambodia relations since the midpoint of the Biden administration, as Phnom Penh has sought to diversify its foreign relations and the U.S. has worked to pull the country out of China’s orbit.
However, the rapprochement has gained inexorable momentum since the inauguration of the second Trump administration, whose transactional mode of diplomacy has been much more to Phnom Penh’s liking. In particular, President Donald Trump’s decision to shutter USAID and cut off U.S. funding for democracy promotion efforts and media outlets like Radio Free Asia removed a key impediment to improved relations on the Cambodian side. As I noted in 2025, Cambodia’s government finally has what it has always wanted: “a relationship with the U.S. that strengthens, rather than undermines, the CPP’s hold on power.”
Last June, the U.S. government officially removed Cambodia from its arms sale blacklist, a month after an American ship docked for the first time at Cambodia’s Ream Naval Base. The latter was particularly significant, given the extensive Chinese refurbishment of the base, which U.S. and Western officials feared was intended to host a permanent Chinese military presence. Adm. Samuel Paparo, commander of the United States Indo-Pacific Command, described the port visit as a sign of the “strong upward trajectory” of relations between Phnom Penh and Washington.
These improvements have come even as branches of the U.S. government have come to officially recognize the extent of the Cambodian elite’s involvement in the country’s gigantic online scamming industry. According to U.S. government agencies, online scamming cost U.S. citizens at least $10 billion in 2024.

articles.title: Is BRICS Actually Benefiting India?
articles.full_text:
As India prepares to host the group’s summit, what does it want from BRICS? And what is Delhi actually getting from the group?
All eyes are on India right now. From September 12 to 13, presidents and prime ministers from Brazil, China, South Africa, Egypt, Indonesia, Russia, and more will converge on New Delhi for the 18th BRICS summit.
It’s India’s fourth time hosting BRICS, but leading the group today is a diplomatic minefield. Barely two months after Delhi took over as chair, the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran, a BRICS member. Tehran then retaliated against the UAE and Saudi Arabia – also BRICS members. Now, India has to sit all three in the same room.
The U.S.-Iran war made it impossible to ignore the serious conflicts within BRICS. In a major diplomatic fail, the BRICS foreign ministers’ meeting in May, also hosted by India, ended without a joint statement. The group’s members just couldn’t agree on how to approach the crisis in West Asia. 
Some worry that the upcoming BRICS summit will also end without a joint statement. That would be a huge embarrassment for the host, India – and something Delhi is keen to avoid. 
In 2021, the last time India hosted the annual summit, BRICS was just five countries, the ones that form its name: Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa.
Today, it’s an unwieldy 11-member bloc – or 10, depending on whether Saudi Arabia ever formally confirms it joined. Reaching a consensus was already tough when it was just India and China at odds within the group; now, BRICS includes rivals actively shooting at each other.
What does India get out of BRICS? And are the benefits worth the growing headache?

articles.title: India’s Cross-Border Cyber Scams Against the US and the West
articles.full_text:
In poor areas such as Jamtara and Mewat, cyber scams have become an important source of household income.
India has become one of the largest global sources of cross-border cyber scams. Its significance extends well beyond the economic losses involved.
Research from the Indian Institute of Technology-Kanpur estimates that Indian call-center fraud causes approximately $10 billion in annual losses worldwide, with victims concentrated in the United States, the United Kingdom, Australia, and Canada. Cryptocurrency “pig-butchering” schemes inside India alone exceeded $3.6 billion in losses in 2024, and losses directly traced to India from U.S. victims between 2023 and 2025 reached $42 million – only the traceable fraction.
Geographically, the Indian scam landscape shows a dual-track structure. A decentralized rural track, epitomized by the Jamtara–Mewat crime belt, accounts for the bulk of the crime. Bharatpur in Rajasthan records the nation’s highest cybercrime rate at 18 percent of reported cases; the Mewat region spanning Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh, and Haryana accounts for 11 percent, and these areas, together with Jamtara, source roughly 80 percent of the country’s cases.
The Mewat model requires no technical skill – only a phone and a bank account – with operators as young as 12 and more than 500 new scams launched daily.
Four criminal methods dominate the industry. Technical support scams, the most iconic export of Indian cybercrime, involve operators impersonating Microsoft or Apple staff, manufacturing fake “virus” or “account intrusion” alerts to lure victims into granting remote access before draining their bank accounts.
As FBI Agent Jeremy Capello has observed, the core mechanism is manufactured technological panic. Government-agency impersonation sees scammers posing as IRS, Social Security, or immigration officials, demanding payment to “clear the charges.” A 2022 U.S. District Court indictment in the Northern District of Georgia revealed multiple Indian call centers routing tens of millions of such calls to American consumers. A newer “digital arrest” scam, in which scammers brandish fake police uniforms and forged warrants on video calls to demand transfers, is now expanding overseas: over 92,000 victims were identified inside India in 2024 alone.
Behind these methods lies a sophisticated infrastructure. The networks route SIP-protocol VoIP calls through multiple servers to obscure their origins, rely on roughly 850,000 mass-purchased “money mule” accounts opened with false Know Your Customer or KYC documents, and move funds across borders through the hawala underground remittance system and cryptocurrencies. An analysis by India’s Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) of more than 15,000 IP addresses found some masterminds based in Southeast Asia while Indian personnel handle calling and account operations – evidence of a cross-continental division of labor.
What makes the Indian case distinctive, however, is the grey connection between the scam syndicates and the political and institutional system. In economically backward areas such as Jamtara and Mewat, cyber scams have become a main source of household income, and local politicians protect voters – and thereby protect votes. Randheer Singh, a member of the legislative assembly of the Bharatiya Janata Party for Jamtara and a former minister, stated in a recorded interview that he frequently has to “make recommendations” to the police to secure the release of arrested voters, threatening to surround the police station if his constituency’s residents are harassed. The arrangement provides scammers with “electoral asylum” without legislators ever participating in the fraud directly.
Institutional complicity extends into the banking and telecommunications networks the scams depend on. In January 2025, Hyderabad police disclosed that a 60-year-old woman had lent her NGO’s bank account to a scam network for a commission of $201,100. When police sought an arrest warrant, ten lawyers appeared in court to defend her.
In February 2025, Indore police documented a father-son pair from an Islamic seminary lending their institution’s accounts for a 50 percent commission. “Ghost SIM cards” provide another conduit: by November 2024, Indian authorities had blocked approximately 669,000 cybercrime-linked SIMs, and Hyderabad’s “Operation Octopus 3.0” in May 2026 seized 1,194 SIMs issued under the identities of ordinary citizens—and even the deceased.
These vulnerabilities are compounded by a structural failure in law enforcement. Police from across India flock to Mewat and Jamtara to arrest suspects, while local forces keep almost no record of proactive enforcement against scam dens in their own jurisdictions.
A 2024 UNODC report identified “selective inaction” by police in high-crime areas as a core driver of the networks’ expansion – a pattern that functions as structural protection without requiring proof of individual bribes. This model contrasts sharply with Southeast Asia, where Cambodia and Myanmar feature direct participation by political and military elites and “nationalized crime.” Instead, India exhibits passive protection by local councilors and grassroots police, vote-driven patronage and a state often simply unable to conduct effective crackdowns.
The U.S. has borne the deepest damage. According to the FBI’s IC3 2025 report, American fraud complaints surpassed one million in 2025 for the first time, with total losses exceeding $20 billion, up from $16.6 billion in 2024. Losses from technical support scams, a major Indian-origin category, climbed from $807 million in 2022 to $1.464 billion in 2024, reaching approximately $2.1 billion in 2025. Victims are highly concentrated among the elderly: in 2024, victims aged 60 and older filed 147,000 complaints totaling $4.8 billion—29 percent of all national cybercrime losses.
U.S. law enforcement has responded with a series of crackdowns. A 2024 joint FBI operation  gainst Indian transnational call centers produced 215 arrests, a 700 percent year-on-year increase. In February 2025, Indian-American operator Hitesh Madhubhai Patel was sentenced in Texas to 20 years in prison and nearly $9 million in restitution. In a February 2026 case in Maryland, three Indian call centers were shown to have caused $48 million in losses to more than 650 victims.
Other Western countries report similar losses. Australia’s reported fraud losses rebounded to $1.57 billion in 2025, up 7.8 percent from 2024, with victims aged 65 and older losing $71.7 million in 2024—the highest absolute loss of any age group.
In Canada, reported fraud losses reached $461 million in 2024, but with a reporting rate of only 5 to 10 percent, implying true losses of $4.34 billion to $9.18 billion.  Government-impersonation scams are among the fastest-growing categories there, with India as the primary source country.
In the United Kingdom, tech-support scams rank among the fastest-growing fraud types, while the absence of European-level data specifically tracking India-sourced scams remains a monitoring gap.
Beyond the economic costs, the hidden damages are substantial. Elderly victims in particular suffer severe psychological trauma: anxiety, depression, social isolation, and self-blame. The systematic impersonation of government agencies erodes public trust, as seniors grow wary of legitimate communications from bodies such as the Social Security Administration. Because the targeted elderly victims are frequently the holders of lifetime savings or intended inheritances, the scams also disrupt intergenerational wealth transfer.
Ultimately, India’s scam industry is driven by the synergy of “employment substitution” and regulatory arbitrage: a large population of educated, English-fluent, underemployed youth provides a continuous labor supply for scam call centers, and in areas lacking formal jobs, fraud has become a “career choice” with its own social-reproduction logic. The grey connections between syndicates and officials represent an economy-driven patronage embedded in a democratic electoral system – an institutional failure of state capacity rather than the proactive criminalization of the state seen in Southeast Asia.
Joint operations such as the FBI–CBI Chakra series deliver short-term wins, but as long as rural underemployment and local electoral patronage persist, they remain “whack-a-mole” tactical successes.

articles.title: The Illusion of Technocratic Transformation in Cambodia
articles.full_text:
The country is hitting a developmental wall because necessary structural reforms clash directly with the needs of an entrenched patronage system.
Cambodian Prime Minister Hun Manet takes part in a meeting of the Central Committee of the Cambodian People’s Party (CPP) in Phnom Penh, Cambodia, January 26, 2025.
Over the past 25 years, Cambodia successfully cut its poverty rate from over 50 percent to under 20 percent. However, the model driving this success now faces severe headwinds. Due to ongoing global price shocks and a sharp, year-long slump in remittances prompted by the Cambodian-Thai border dispute, more than a million people risk falling back below the subsistence level, according to the World Bank. This vulnerability underscores the fragility of Cambodia’s growth model. Without structurally transforming the domestic economy, hard-won social progress remains in jeopardy.
In its June 2026 Cambodia Economic Update, the World Bank painted its usual optimistic picture of macroeconomic resilience with projected GDP growth of 3.9 percent in 2026 and 4.9 percent in 2027 amid rising exports and accelerating momentum in new industrial sectors. Yet these signs of progress conceal a deep structural problem: Cambodia remains a dual economy.
On the one hand, the country boasts a highly productive export sector, dominated almost entirely by foreign, primarily Chinese, investment, which manufactures garments and footwear for global companies. This side of the economy operates largely as an enclave, relying on few domestic factors other than cheap labor. On the other hand, a fragmented and technologically deficient domestic economy consists largely of small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) that struggle to compete internationally and remain concentrated in the informal sector. In 2022, 90 percent of all businesses fell into this category, yet they generated only about 40-45 percent of GDP, according to World Bank statistics.
Cambodia Could Fall Into the Middle-Income Trap
All of this points to the exhaustion of Cambodia’s existing growth model. The purely quantitative shift of labor from subsistence farming into textile factories – the classic “reallocation dividend” described by the Lewis model – is no longer generating significant productivity gains. To avoid falling into a middle-income trap, Cambodia must turn FDI into a vehicle for technology and knowledge transfer to the domestic economy. The middle-income trap occurs when countries escape poverty but then stagnate: rising wages erode their advantage in low-cost labor, while they lack the innovation capacity needed to compete with advanced economies.
Should East African nations, particularly Ethiopia and Kenya, boost their competitiveness in the coming years, Cambodia could face intensified pressure in labor-intensive export industries. Domestic pressures are also mounting, driven by what the World Bank anticipates to be the inevitable closure of Cambodia’s demographic window around 2043. Currently, the country benefits from an exceptionally young population and a temporary surplus of working-age people. However, if Cambodia fails over the next two decades to equip this generation with the skills it needs through substantial investment in education and to integrate young workers into higher-value supply chains, the country risks growing old before it becomes prosperous.
In its update, the World Bank recommended a three-stage reform: safeguarding subsistence farms through social protection; boosting SME productivity through better credit access and digitalization; and formalizing high-performing local businesses to help them qualify as suppliers to major foreign investors.
However, this economically sound solution reflects a purely technocratic understanding of Cambodia. It treats the country as a rational institutional landscape while ignoring its political economy. The country’s real obstacle is not a lack of administrative guidelines or digital portals, but the deeply entrenched system of patronage and oligopoly that has developed under the ruling Cambodian People’s Party (CPP) and significantly constrains market efficiency and innovative entrepreneurship.
The Elite Pact and the Limits of Innovation
In Cambodia, economic success depends less on productivity or innovation than on proximity to political power. This system, closely resembling the crony capitalism of Suharto’s Indonesia and Marcos’ Philippines, is institutionalized within the Oknha class – an oligarchic economic elite that secures exclusive market access, state land concessions, and protection from foreign competition through million-dollar donations to the regime.
This elite pact fundamentally distorts entrepreneurial risk. Large domestic conglomerates, such as the Royal Group, Canadia/OCIC, Chip Mong, or the LYP Group, focus heavily on protected, domestic-market-oriented sectors like real estate, financial services, gambling, telecommunications, and trade. While not all of these entrepreneurs lack productivity, the institutional environment rewards political rent-seeking rather than competitive, global industrial value chains. For a Cambodian oligarch, making high-risk, multimillion-dollar investments in R&D or high-precision manufacturing is simply not economically attractive.
Politically safeguarded rent-seeking in a protected domestic market offers a far more lucrative risk-return profile than fierce international competition against regional rivals. Simultaneously, this system stifles the productive middle class. Independent, innovative SMEs find it nearly impossible to scale up. If they break into profitable niches, they risk having their business models appropriated by politically connected actors, as property rights in Cambodia remain poorly protected without political patronage. Under such conditions, qualified Cambodians seek advancement mainly in the civil service or the military, two arenas where power easily translates into personal gain.
Cambodia Lags Behind in Regional Comparisons
When seeking solutions, international analyses frequently point to regional success stories, particularly Malaysia and Vietnam. Yet these comparisons serve only to highlight Cambodia’s severe shortcomings. This institutional gap is vividly reflected in the Bertelsmann Transformation Index (BTI). While Cambodia has scored the absolute lowest mark of 1 out of 10 in anti-corruption policy since 2018, Vietnam (5 points) and Malaysia (6 points) remain on an entirely different institutional trajectory.
According to BTI criteria, Cambodia’s minimum score indicates a total failure to control corruption, with core integrity mechanisms – such as independent public expenditure audits, official accountability mechanisms, or transparent procurement systems – effectively non-existent. While Vietnam and Malaysia also display functional shortcomings, they maintain established core mechanisms that guarantee businesses at least a basic level of institutional predictability. These quantitative discrepancies have fundamentally crippled the country’s economic dynamics.
The prime historical example of overcoming this form of dual economy is Malaysia’s Penang region. In the 1970s, Malaysia faced similar enclave challenges that Cambodia encounters today. Building on a more professional bureaucracy, Malaysia broke this enclave structure through three approaches: a targeted cluster policy; state-run matchmaking agencies like the Penang Development Corporation, which guided local firms toward multinational corporations’ quality standards; and the Penang Skill Development Centre, a state-funded education hub managed directly by foreign tech giants. Cambodia, by contrast, lacks both the institutional capacity for such matchmaking and an education system aligned with real-world market needs.
Conversely, Vietnam, with its socialist-oriented market economy, outperforms Cambodia in strategically coordinating economic actors. Although links between FDI and its local economy remain weak, Hanoi has countered this with an assertive, state-led industrial policy and a relatively effective anti-corruption campaign. Rather than leaving the market to its own devices, Hanoi deliberately cultivates state-affiliated conglomerates like Vingroup or Viettel to act as spearheads of its industrial strategy. In exchange for market access, the government leverages these “national champions” to demand technology transfers from global giants like Samsung or Intel. In contrast, Cambodia’s laissez-faire approach in its Special Economic Zones leaves such matchmaking entirely to a flawed market, where local inefficiencies prevent it from ever taking place.
Political Implications and Necessary Measures
The generational transition from long-serving Prime Minister Hun Sen to his son Hun Manet has done little to alter the existing political dynamics in Cambodia. While the Western-educated, second-generation CPP cadres push for superficial modernization and administrative digitalization, the underlying political deal remains untouched: the Oknhas continue to bankroll the regime’s grip on power in exchange for the protection of their domestic fiefdoms. Hence, dismantling the dual economy requires more than new, technocratic reform packages; it demands a fundamental realignment of economic incentives with measurable conditions that do not fundamentally conflict with the regime’s political interests.
First, the government must stop shielding domestic monopolies. State concessions, loans, and licenses for domestic conglomerates should be strictly contingent on international competitiveness and export revenues. Those who fail in the global market must lose their political protection.
The second priority is to create a genuinely meritocratic civil service. As long as posts in key ministries and regulatory bodies are bought or inherited at exorbitant prices, SME support is doomed to fail. Subsidies and administrative aid must be managed by a professionalized, merit-based civil service, isolated from dysfunctional patronage networks.
Finally, the government must recognize that relying purely on SEZs for diversification is no longer enough. To break the dual economy, the government must offer tax incentives to foreign investors who enter long-term joint ventures with local firms, ensure technology transfers, and promote local talent to management positions. Simultaneously, physical technology clusters must logistically and geographically link local suppliers to anchor multinational corporations.
As long as the systemic logic of elite distribution dominates economic policy, technocratic proposals like those that the World Bank has suggested for years will remain insufficient. The case of Cambodia proves that sustainable economic modernization is inextricably linked to the quality of governance. A political transformation grounded in the rule of law and oriented toward the common good is a mandatory prerequisite to prevent the market order from becoming a mere façade. Without shifting away from a rent-seeking economic model, Cambodia will miss its chance to become a competitive industrial nation, remaining permanently stuck in a stalled transformation.

articles.title: Schools Close Across Sarawak Due to Toxic Haze From Indonesian Wildfires
articles.full_text:
Wildfires have raged for weeks across swathes of Sumatra and Kalimantan, exacerbated by a particularly severe dry season.
Transboundary haze hangs over the city of Alor Setar, the capital of Kedah State in peninsular Malaysia, Oct. 3, 2015.
Hundreds of schools across the Malaysian state of Sarawak have closed their doors because of hazardous haze from ongoing wildfires in neighboring Indonesia.
Sarawak, which runs along the north of the island of Borneo, is currently under a pall of air pollution that is among the worst it has seen this decade. On September 3, Malaysian authorities declared an emergency in Serian Division, a region in the southwest of Sarawak bordering Indonesia, after air pollution levels hit critical levels.
King Sultan Ibrahim “has consented to the declaration of emergency throughout Serian Division, Sarawak, following haze conditions that have reached air pollution levels hazardous to public health and safety,” Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s office said in a statement on September 3.
“The government will continue to monitor developments from time to time and ensure that all necessary actions are implemented immediately, including mitigation measures and the dissemination of information and health advice to the public,” it added.
Under the emergency measures, government and private offices in the town of Serian will be closed, as well as plantations, construction sites, and quarries, the AFP news agency reported. The Sarawak Disaster Management Committee also announced a three-day cloud-seeding operation that was subsequently extended to today.
On Friday, authorities also announced that 647 schools across 12 districts, including Serian and the state capital Kuching, will close their doors this week, moving lessons to an online format. A further 54 primary schools and nine secondary schools in Bintulu Division further to the east will also shut their doors due to haze, the Sarawak Education Department announced on Saturday.
The Sarawak Disaster Management Committee formally requested the declaration when the Air Pollutant Index (API) in Serian soared into dangerous territory, peaking at 519 on Friday. The Malaysian government considers API levels above 300 to be “hazardous” to human health, while readings beyond 500 justify the announcement of an emergency declaration. The Malaysia Meteorological Department told Channel News Asia (CNA) that this is Sarawak’s “worst” haze episode since 2019.
The deteriorating air quality has disrupted daily life across Sarawak. According to CNA, “outdoor events, including carnivals, community runs and sporting activities, have been cancelled, while poor visibility has disrupted some flights.”
“Transboundary haze” has become a seasonal crisis in large parts of Southeast Asia, in line with the expansion of agricultural monocultures such as palm oil, maize, paper pulp, and sugar. These are compounded by vehicle and industrial emissions and naturally occurring dry-season forest fires.
This year, the main cause is the wildfires that have raged for weeks across Indonesia’s Sumatra and Kalimantan regions, exacerbated by a particularly severe dry season. The Ministry of Forestry says that wildfires burned at least 202,010 hectares of land from January to July, around half of which took place in the month of July.
The ASEAN Specialized Meteorological Centre reported on Friday that “moderate smoke plumes were … observed to emanate from hotspots in the southern parts of Kalimantan and the southern and central parts of Sumatra.” There have also been reports of fires in South Papua, which has not traditionally seen many dry season fires. One environmentalist told CNA that this was likely “linked to land clearing in food estate and energy project areas.”
While bordering areas of Sarawak have been hardest hit by the poisonous haze, the pollution has also spread to Sabah and peninsular Malaysia, Brunei, and as far as the Philippines. On Friday, Singapore also announced it would start providing daily haze advisories from Friday evening, after the 24-hour air quality readings entered the unhealthy range for the first time since 2023.
Indonesian authorities suspect that most of the fires in Kalimantan and Sumatra were deliberately set by individuals or companies for various purposes, Forestry Minister Raja Juli Antoni said last week.
“It is almost certain that the cause is deliberate burning, not wildfires, whether carried out by individuals, ordinary farmers, or corporations,” Raja told a press conference on September 1, the Jakarta Globe reported.
Rizal Irawan, a senior official at the country’s Environment Ministry, told Reuters that the authorities were investigating 19 companies that it believes may be linked to the wildfires, and said that it would investigate who might be responsible.
“Regardless of the cause, strict liability applies whenever a fire occurs within a concession area,” he said.
While API readings in Serian have dropped since the state of emergency came into effect – the reading as of press time was 162, in the merely “very unhealthy” zone – Indonesian authorities say that there is no immediate relief on the horizon.
Raja said that the month of September is expected to mark a critical period in efforts to contain fires due to intensifying El Niño conditions.
“We must remain extremely vigilant because, for me, September is when the real battle begins,” Raja said, according to the Jakarta Globe. “September is the peak of El Niño, so we have to stay alert.”

articles.title: What’s Happening in Philippine Vice President Sara Duterte’s Impeachment Trial?
articles.full_text:
The trial has dropped from the headlines amid ongoing corruption controversies and the massive flooding that hit vast areas of Luzon this month.
Philippine senators take part in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, Sept. 2, 2026.
This week marks the second month of the impeachment trial of Philippine Vice President Sara Duterte, who is accused of betrayal of public trust over the alleged misuse of public funds, accumulation of unexplained wealth, and making grave threats against the president. What has happened over the past two months, and what’s the prospect of her conviction or acquittal?
Two articles of the impeachment complaint have been presented already to the public. The first accusation refers to her involvement in a conspiracy to assassinate President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. The second issue, which is considered by anti-corruption advocates as the main aspect of the case, is about Duterte’s anomalous spending of confidential funds.
Perhaps the prosecution decided to prioritize the presentation of the issue of grave threats to galvanize and unite the president’s constituency. The evidence was clear even if Duterte’s camp tried hard to undermine the testimony of the witnesses from law enforcement bodies. Duterte’s defense tactic is expected to double down on the argument about the vice president exercising her freedom of speech.
As expected, the confidential funds issue has produced old and new documentary evidence showing the irregular spending of Duterte’s office. The prosecution is not yet done presenting the case, and they could follow this up by highlighting the suspicious bank transactions made by Duterte and her husband. Based on the line of questioning and earlier manifestations of Duterte’s legal team, they could try to link the questionable use of funds to the counterinsurgency operations of security forces. They could also assert the inadmissibility of evidence by citing bank secrecy laws.
Duterte is not required to appear at the trial, but she has been called out for her absence while disparaging her accusers in her public appearances. In particular, she has lambasted prosecutors for “fishing for evidence” and concocting “wild stories” of alleged wrongdoing. The defense panel has also criticized some prosecutors for posting offensive remarks on social media.
The impeachment is more than just a legal process; it is a political mechanism designed to hold officials accountable. A vicious exchange of political rhetoric from both parties and other stakeholders is intended to gather public support. Nevertheless, the presiding officer issued a ruling that prohibited all those directly involved in the trial from commenting about the case. The ruling covers Duterte, which might restrict her ability to argue her case and influence public opinion.
After two months, there have been suggestions to shorten the duration of the trial. The prosecution is studying the option of foregoing the presentation of other articles of impeachment since they believe they have already made a solid case for the conviction of Duterte. It could also mean that they wanted to expedite the trial to sustain public interest. A crucial decision point is the legal assertion by some lawmakers to lower the number of votes required to convict Duterte, since some senator-judges have been unable to participate in the proceedings because they have been detained over corruption charges. Another senator-judge has left the country and is reportedly seeking medical treatment. This legal question could reach the Supreme Court and potentially make a huge impact on the case and the country’s politics ahead of the 2028 elections.
Contrary to initial impressions, it is not impeachment matters that have dominated recent political debates but the unresolved corruption controversies and the massive flooding that hit vast areas of Luzon, the country’s biggest island. This was less because the impeachment was less interesting than the fact that residents had to prioritize survival amid rising floodwaters and point out the continuing failure to hold accountable the corrupt officials implicated in the infrastructure scam. It didn’t help that the draft budget bill for 2027 retained fund items that can be used for political patronage and pork barrel distribution.
As the nation marks the first anniversary of last year’s widespread anti-corruption protests, residents in flooded communities are joined by concerned citizens who are outraged over the continuing impunity and the apparent failure or reluctance of the Marcos government to overhaul the budget system that enabled the systematic stealing of the country’s resources.
Duterte might try to echo the public discontent against the entrenched corruption in the bureaucracy to divert attention from her trial, but she has no credibility in leading the advocacy for good governance. She is a target of the citizen-led anti-corruption movement, which is demanding accountability from the country’s two highest officials.

This week marks the second month of the impeachment trial of Philippine Vice President Sara Duterte, who is accused of betrayal of public trust over the alleged misuse of public funds, accumulation of unexplained wealth, and making grave threats against the president. What has happened over the past two months, and what’s the prospect of her conviction or acquittal?
Two articles of the impeachment complaint have been presented already to the public. The first accusation refers to her involvement in a conspiracy to assassinate President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. The second issue, which is considered by anti-corruption advocates as the main aspect of the case, is about Duterte’s anomalous spending of confidential funds.

The evidence was clear even if Duterte’s camp tried hard to undermine the testimony of the witnesses from law enforcement bodies. Duterte’s defense tactic is expected to double down on the argument about the vice president exercising her freedom of speech.

articles.title: Myanmar President Min Aung Hlaing Concludes State Visit to Vietnam
articles.full_text:
The two nations agreed to bolster cooperation in a host of areas, including defense, investment, trade, and digital technologies.
Myanmar’s military-appointed President Min Aung Hlaing yesterday wound up a three-day visit to Vietnam, during which he and Hanoi’s top leaders agreed to expand cooperation across a broad front.
The former general arrived in Vietnam on Friday, part of a diplomatic campaign aimed at consolidating ties with regional governments and normalizing relations with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN).
In addition to meeting top leaders including President To Lam and Prime Minister Le Minh Hung, Min Aung Hlaing also held meetings with top Vietnamese firms such as VinFast, a local EV manufacturer, ​and the military-run telecoms group Viettel, which operates Mytel, one of Myanmar’s major telecom operators.
According to a Vietnamese government statement quoted by Reuters, a key focus of the talks between Lam and Min Aung Hlaing was defense and security cooperation, which the two leaders elevated to a key pillar of bilateral ties.
In particular, the two leaders “agreed to expand cooperation in military training, exchanges between young officers, search-and-rescue operations and ​disaster response, while stepping up information sharing and coordination ​against crimes,” the statement said.
“Vietnam stands ⁠ready to share its experience in national development, ensuring economic ​security and fostering sustainable growth,” the statement quoted Lam as saying during the talks.
Economics and trade were also high on the agenda. Trade between the two nations has fallen in recent years, as Myanmar has become engulfed in civil conflict. According to statistics cited by the Associated Press, two-way trade totaled $853 million in 2020 but then fell to $590 million in 2025.
Speaking at the Myanmar-Viet Nam Business Forum in Hanoi yesterday, Min Aung Hlaing called “for greater bilateral economic cooperation and increased Vietnamese investment in Myanmar,” the Global New Light of Myanmar reported. In particular, he said that Myanmar was “seeking to expand cooperation with Vietnam in telecommunications, technology, manufacturing, agriculture, energy, tourism and human resources development,” in the newspaper’s paraphrase.
Both sides also reaffirmed a commitment not to allow any individual or organization to use one country’s territory ​for activities against the other – a similar arrangement to the one that Lam made during his visit to Thailand in May.
During his meeting with Min Aung Hlaing on Saturday, Le Minh Hung “congratulated Myanmar on achieving significant results in national governance under the leadership of President Min Aung Hlaing,” Vietnamese state media reported. He also “affirmed Vietnam’s support for the Myanmar government in continuing to implement measures to promote stability, reconciliation, dialogue, economic development, and improve people’s lives.”
Vietnam was the eighth country that Min ‌Aung Hlaing has visited since taking office in April, and the third member state from ASEAN, with a fourth – Cambodia – to follow later this week. He has also paid visits to India, China, Russia, Belarus, and Kazakhstan. In all of these places, he has sought to consolidate diplomatic relationships and to drum up foreign investment, as evidenced by the large business and political delegations that have accompanied him on each trip.
A top priority, which Min Aung Hlaing flagged in his inauguration speech in April, is to normalize relations with ASEAN, which since late 2021 has excluded the country from its summits over its failure to implement the bloc’s Five-Point Consensus conflict resolution plan. This plan calls for a cessation of violence, access to humanitarian aid, and inclusive dialogue involving “all parties” to the country’s conflict.
Myanmar’s government has rejected the Consensus, in both word and deed, while cultivating relations with those ASEAN member states most sympathetic to its reintegration into the 11-nation bloc.

articles.title: Free and Open Indo-Pacific: A Pillar of Deeper Regional Cooperation
articles.full_text:
Japan’s Indo-Pacific vision has outlasted its creator and found new partners. Beijing is not pleased.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio meets with Indo-Pacific Quad Foreign Ministers in Manila, Philippines, July 22, 2026.
In July 2026, the foreign ministers of the Quad countries — Japan, the United States, Australia, and India — met on the sidelines of the ASEAN Foreign Ministers’ Meeting in Manila and issued the “Joint Press Release on Quad Cooperation with ASEAN,” reaffirming their support for ASEAN centrality and unity and the “ASEAN Outlook on the Indo-Pacific (AOIP).” The Quad foreign ministers also reaffirmed their commitment to a “Free and Open Indo-Pacific (FOIP)” and outlined their intention to deepen cooperation with ASEAN, with FOIP as a core pillar.
It has been ten years since former Prime Minister Shinzo Abe proposed the FOIP at the Sixth Tokyo International Conference on African Development (TICAD VI) in Nairobi, Kenya, in August 2016. Abe viewed Asia and Africa, and the Pacific and Indian Oceans, as an inseparable and integrated region, and expressed Japan’s determination to maintain “freedom from coercion,” the “rule of law,” and a “market economy” across it. The FOIP philosophy won broad acceptance across the Indo-Pacific, from advanced Western nations such as the United States and Australia to developing countries including African nations, India, and ASEAN member states. In June 2019, ASEAN adopted the AOIP as its own Indo-Pacific vision, guided by principles including ASEAN centrality, inclusiveness, and respect for international law.
In promoting FOIP, Japan has placed particular emphasis on cooperation with ASEAN. Southeast Asia is a strategically vital region connecting the Pacific and Indian Oceans, and one facing pressure to change the status quo by force or coercion. Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi attended the Japan-ASEAN Summit in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, in October 2025. At the meeting, she stated Japan’s commitment to safeguarding the peace, stability, and prosperity of the Indo-Pacific together with ASEAN, by evolving FOIP — a core pillar of Japanese diplomacy — and deepening synergy with the AOIP.
Following the summit, the leaders of Japan and ASEAN issued the “Joint Statement on the Further Promotion and Implementation of the AOIP.” Reaffirming that Japan’s FOIP and the AOIP “share relevant fundamental principles,” the statement affirmed that implementing the AOIP contributes to a rules-based international order and a free and open Indo-Pacific. It also welcomed “Japan’s efforts to promote cooperation rather than division and confrontation through the FOIP.” The statement reflected a shared commitment by Japan and ASEAN to support both frameworks and to cooperate for Indo-Pacific stability and prosperity on the basis of shared principles.
When Takaichi visited Hanoi, Vietnam, in May 2026, she delivered a speech at Vietnam National University outlining the “Updated FOIP.” She asserted that ten years on, the case for FOIP remains as strong as ever, and that Japan will continue working toward an international order based on “freedom,” “openness,” “diversity,” “inclusiveness,” and the “rule of law.” She identified structural changes in the international order — “intensifying geopolitical competition,” “accelerated technological innovation,” and the “rise of the Global South” — and stressed the need to adapt FOIP accordingly. She expressed her determination to drive the updated FOIP with a focus on three priority areas: (1) building economic infrastructure for the AI and data era, (2) co-creating economic growth opportunities and sharing rules, and (3) enhancing cooperation in the security field.
The updated FOIP was also welcomed at the Quad Foreign Ministers’ Meeting held in New Delhi, India, in late May. The Quad foreign ministers reaffirmed their support for a FOIP that enables countries to develop resilience and strengthen autonomy, and announced four concrete initiatives toward its realization: (1) maritime and transnational security, (2) economic prosperity and security, (3) critical and emerging technology, and (4) humanitarian assistance and emergency response. Quad cooperation grounded in FOIP has visibly deepened.
That the Quad Foreign Ministers’ Meeting was held alongside the ASEAN Foreign Ministers’ Meeting in July 2026, and expressed its support for the AOIP, is a clear signal that cooperation among Japan, the United States, Australia, India, and ASEAN — with FOIP as a core pillar — continues to advance. A spokesperson for China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs criticized the updated FOIP as a “sugarcoated scheme that sows division and rivalry” and claimed it “will never win genuine recognition from regional countries.” Ten years after its inception, with broad and deepening support across the Indo-Pacific, the FOIP record speaks for itself.
